title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather — the number one small-talk topic in a country where it changes constantly — and master sentences that have no subject at all.
bekal: tell *on kylmä* (it's cold out) from *minulla on kylmä* (I'm cold)
name the four seasons, temperatures and the clothes worn in each

dialogs.title: Dialog — Ensimmäinen talvi
dialogs.intro: Early November. Budi is having his first snowy day. Aino calls.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Hei Budi! Millainen sää siellä on?
lines.id: Hi Budi! What's the weather like there?
lines.literal: hi Budi! what-kind weather there is?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: It's snowing! For the first time in my life.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: On. Ulkona on miinus kuusi astetta. Ja minulla on kylmä.
lines.id: Yes. It's minus six degrees outside. And I'm cold.
lines.literal: is. outside is minus six degree-part. and at-me is cold.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Kaksi eri asiaa! Onko sinulla oikeat vaatteet?
lines.id: Two different things! Do you have the right clothes?
lines.literal: two different thing-part! is-? at-you right clothes?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En tiedä. Minulla on takki ja hanskat.
lines.id: I don't know. I have a jacket and gloves.
lines.literal: not-I know. at-me is jacket and gloves.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Tarvitset villasukat ja pipon. Pää palelee ensimmäisenä.
lines.id: You need wool socks and a beanie. Your head gets cold first.
lines.literal: need-you wool-socks and beanie-whole. head freezes as-first.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Mutta kesällä aurinko paistaa yölläkin. Se korvaa kaiken.
lines.id: But in summer the sun shines even at night. That makes up for everything.
lines.literal: but in-summer sun shines at-night-even. it replaces everything.

notes: **Sataa lunta has no subject at all.** No "it" as in English *it's snowing*. The verb stands alone in the *hän* form, and that's already a complete sentence. Leaving out the "it" is the hardest part for English speakers — resist the urge to add *se*.

**On kylmä and minulla on kylmä are two different things.** The first is about the weather, the second about your body. Aino corrects Budi in line 5 because he mixed them up. In English the difference is only "it's" vs "I'm"; in Finnish the whole structure changes.
**Miinus kuusi astetta** — a temperature below zero. You can also say *kuusi astetta pakkasta* ("six degrees of frost"), which sounds more Finnish. Above zero: *kuusi astetta lämmintä*.
**Ensimmäisenä** — the *-na/-nä* ending again, the same one used with days. Here it means "as the first". This ending really is versatile; its third use comes in unit 18.

**Yölläkin** = *yöllä* + *-kin* ("too"). *-kin* attaches to any word and means "too, even": *minäkin* (me too), *tänäänkin* (today too). Its counterpart *-kaan/-kään* is used in negative sentences: *en minäkään* (me neither).

**Kesällä aurinko paistaa yöllä** is not a figure of speech. In Helsinki in late June the sun sets around 10:50 p.m. and rises again at 3:55 a.m.; in Lapland it doesn't set at all for weeks. In winter, by contrast, Lapland has *kaamos* — the sun doesn't rise at all.

grammars.title: Weather sentences — sentences without a subject
body: In Finnish, weather is expressed with a bare verb in the *hän* form, without a single word saying who or what is doing it.
after: ⚠️ Notice the two adjective forms: *on kylmä* (basic form) but *on pilvis**tä***, *on sumuis**ta***, *on liukas**ta*** (partial). Adjectives ending in *-inen* and *-as* take the partial form in weather sentences. At A1, just learn the common ones as they are.
What falls is partial: *sataa vet**tä***, *sataa lun**ta***, *sataa räntä**ä*** (sleet). You already know why — rain never falls "in full".
Asking: *Millainen sää on?* (what's the weather like?) or *Sataako?* (is it raining?). Answer by repeating the verb: *Sataa.* / *Ei sada.*

grammars.title: Is it cold, or am I cold?
body: Three structures that look alike but point to different things. Learners mix these up constantly, because in English the only change is the subject.
after: You learned *minulla on…* in unit 4 for possession. Here it's used for bodily states, and this use is very wide: *minulla on nälkä* (I'm hungry), *minulla on jano* (I'm thirsty), *minulla on kiire* (I'm in a hurry), *minulla on ikävä* (I miss someone).

⚠️ *Minua paleltaa* puts **you yourself** in the partial form — you're the target, not the doer. The same structure for aches: *minua särkee* (I'm aching), *minua väsyttää* (I'm sleepy). This group comes back in unit 17.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note *kevät → keväällä*: the final *t* disappears and the vowel lengthens. Words ending in *-t* have a mind of their own; *lyhyt → lyhyellä*, *kevät → keväällä*.

blocks.title: What's really hard, and what turns out not to be
items: Newcomers always fear the **cold**. What's actually hard is the **dark**: in Helsinki in late December the sun rises at 9:24 a.m. and sets at 3:13 p.m. The cold can be solved with clothes; the dark can't.
What Finns themselves do: bright lights at home, vitamin D (almost everyone takes it), going outside in the middle of the day even briefly, and sauna.
Good news for newcomers from warm climates: Finnish buildings are very well heated. Indoors it's almost always 21–23 °C, all year round.

blocks.text: Notice that many clothes are **plural** in Finnish, just as in English: *housut* (trousers), *hanskat*, *kengät*, *sukat*. Here English instincts actually help you.

blocks.title: Weather talk — the safest small talk in Finland
items: *Kylmä tänään, vai mitä?* — Cold today, isn't it?
Weather is the one topic that's safe to open with a stranger in Finland. Asking someone you've just met about their job, salary or family feels much more intrusive than in many other cultures.
The air outside is very cold.

exercises.prompt: Change the season into the "in that season" form.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Millainen sää siellä on? — Sataa lunta. — Ulkona on miinus kuusi astetta. — Minulla on kylmä. — Aurinko paistaa. — Milloin talvi loppuu?
On kylmä. — Minulla on kylmä. — On kuuma. — Minulla on kuuma. — Minulla on nälkä. — Minulla on jano.
Tänään sataa lunta. — Minulla on kylmä. — Kesällä aurinko paistaa yöllä. — Ulkona on miinus kuusi astetta. — Millainen sää on?
